attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Captures both parts: the fourfold result went unnoted, and the Esvelt-lab paper got no detailed discussion. 'Shocking' is opinion and is rightly left out.

contract.note: Reading 'noted' as explicitly highlighting the ratio is fair to what Marcus meant. But 'the media' has no defined set and 'in any detail' has no threshold, so the result depends on how wide the record is drawn.

evidence.note: Contemporary Bloomberg report. Neither the fourfold comparison nor the Esvelt study appears, but this is one outlet only.
Contemporary Verge report. It questions OpenAI's framing but does not cite the fourfold ratio or discuss Soice et al. Again, one outlet only.

reviews.rationale: The support condition needs a reasonably complete contemporary record. The packet has only two media articles as evidence items, and the OpenAI publication itself is not included as an item. Both articles are consistent with the claim, but the packet itself says the media search was not exhaustive. That is not enough to settle a claim that covers all of 'the media' and OpenAI.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. Footnote 3 gives the counts.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'for experts' scope and the 'one interpretation' framing. Faithful as a claim about the observed sample proportions.

contract.note: Defining success as an accuracy score of 8 or more and comparing sample proportions matches Marcus's footnote and the study's own threshold analysis. It is a fair, ordinary reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI's primary participant data. It gives the expert denominators: 25 per arm, by the drafter's count. The visible rows are consistent, e.g. ID 22 is an LLM-assisted expert.

OpenAI's primary response scores. Visible rows show formulation scores of 8 for IDs 22 and 64. The derived join gives 4/25 vs 1/25, a ratio of 4. This is the study's own data, which is the right source for a claim about the study.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's published participant and response data, joined by ID, show 4 of 25 LLM-assisted experts and 1 of 25 internet-only experts at or above 8/10 on formulation. That is 16% vs 4%, a fourfold observed ratio, which meets the support condition for the sample-proportion reading.

attribution.note: Marcus's own footnote in his post.

semantics.note: The factual part is checkable. The 'no-no in a journal' judgment is normative and the contract correctly does not grade it.

contract.note: Even on a narrow reading, the main publication's own appendix names the tests used. Including the linked summary only adds the p-values. The result does not hinge on the scope chosen.

evidence.note: Appendix C of the original study names one-sided t-tests and a Mann-Whitney U-test as a check.
OpenAI's linked summary file lists the obtained p-values for each task and total, e.g. 0.0027 for expert total accuracy.

reviews.rationale: The study's appendix identifies the significance tests applied: t-tests plus Mann-Whitney. The linked statistical summary reports the obtained p-values. Both parts of the 'reported neither' claim fail on materials published January 31, 2024.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: An observation about what the study established. The qualifier granting the Bonferroni argument is kept.

contract.note: The plain reading is that the study did not rule out a practically important effect. That is the ordinary meaning and is fair.

evidence.note: The original study reports positive but nonsignificant accuracy gains and failed Barnard tests. It leaves practical importance open. It sets no justified practical threshold and gives no precise estimate that would exclude an important effect.

reviews.rationale: The study shows only nonsignificant differences in a small sample, with gains in the positive direction. It does not show that any positive effect falls below a justified practical threshold. A nonsignificant result does not prove an important effect is absent, so the support condition is met.
